name: Colon (large intestine)
func: The large intestine absorbs water and salts from leftover food, turning liquid waste into solid stool. It also houses trillions of helpful bacteria that ferment fibre and make some vitamins.

levels.kid:
The **colon**, or **large intestine**, is a wide tube that goes around the edge of your tummy like a picture frame: up the right side, across the top, and down the left side.

By the time food reaches the colon, your body has already taken out most of the good stuff. What's left is watery mush. The colon's job is to soak up the water, so the leftovers turn into **poop** that's soft but solid.

The colon is also home to **trillions of tiny bacteria**, more than all the people on Earth many times over! Most of them are friendly. They eat the fibre from fruit and vegetables that you can't digest, make some vitamins for you, and help keep bad germs away. Some of them make gas, which is why you sometimes toot!
levels.hs:
The large intestine is about **1.5 metres** long. It starts at the **caecum** in the right iliac fossa (where the ileum joins and the appendix hangs), then runs:
- **Ascending colon**: up the right side to the **right colic (hepatic) flexure**, under the liver.
- **Transverse colon**: across the upper abdomen, below the stomach, hanging on its own mesentery (the **transverse mesocolon**); the greater omentum drapes down from it.
- **Descending colon**: from the **left colic (splenic) flexure**, near the spleen, down the left side.
- **Sigmoid colon**: an S-shaped loop on its own mesentery in the left iliac fossa and pelvis, leading to the **rectum** at about **S3**.

The ascending and descending colon are **retroperitoneal** (fixed to the back wall, in front of the kidneys); the transverse and sigmoid colon are **intraperitoneal** and mobile.

You can tell colon from small intestine by three features:
- **Taeniae coli**: three ribbon-like bands of longitudinal muscle.
- **Haustra**: pouches formed because the taeniae are shorter than the wall.
- **Appendices epiploicae** (omental appendices): small fatty tags.

It absorbs about 1–1.5 litres of water a day, plus sodium and chloride, and secretes potassium and mucus. Food residue takes roughly 1–3 days to pass through.
levels.college:
**Blood supply** follows the embryonic gut:
- **Midgut** (caecum, ascending colon, proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon): **superior mesenteric artery** via the **ileocolic**, **right colic** and **middle colic** arteries.
- **Hindgut** (distal third of transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, upper rectum): **inferior mesenteric artery (IMA)** via the **left colic**, **sigmoid** and **superior rectal** arteries.
These are linked by the **marginal artery (of Drummond)** along the colon's inner edge, and sometimes by the **arc of Riolan**. The **splenic flexure** is a **watershed area** (Griffiths' point) between SMA and IMA territories, vulnerable to **ischaemic colitis** when blood pressure drops. So is the **rectosigmoid junction** (Sudeck's point).

**Venous** drainage goes to the superior and inferior mesenteric veins and then the **portal vein**.

**Nerves**: midgut parts get parasympathetic fibres from the **vagus**; hindgut parts from the **pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4)**. The transition is at about the distal third of the transverse colon. Pain from midgut colon is felt around the umbilicus, from hindgut colon in the **suprapubic** region.

**Histology**: no villi; straight tubular **crypts** with many **goblet cells**; simple columnar epithelium of absorptive **colonocytes**.

**Motility**: **segmental (haustral) contractions** mix contents slowly, and a few times a day **mass movements** push contents along long stretches, often after a meal (the **gastrocolic reflex**).

**Lymph** follows the arteries to the mesenteric nodes, which is why cancer surgery removes the colon segment together with its artery and nodes.
levels.phd:
**Colonocytes** get most of their energy from **butyrate**, a **short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)** made by bacterial fermentation of dietary fibre. SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) also strengthen the epithelial barrier, drive sodium and water absorption via SCFA–bicarbonate exchange, and act on G-protein receptors (**FFAR2/3**) and as **histone deacetylase inhibitors**, promoting anti-inflammatory **regulatory T cells**.

**Electrolyte transport**: in the distal colon, **ENaC** channels (upregulated by **aldosterone**) absorb sodium, and **BK** channels secrete potassium. The colon's mucus forms two layers: a dense inner layer (built on **MUC2**) that keeps bacteria at a distance, and a loose outer layer they live in.

**Microbiome**: about 10¹¹ bacteria per gram of colonic contents, dominated by **Bacteroidetes** and **Firmicutes**. Bacterial enzymes deconjugate bile acids, make **vitamin K2** and some B vitamins, and produce gases.

**Gut–brain axis**: microbes influence the brain via the **vagus nerve**, immune signalling and metabolites (SCFAs, tryptophan metabolites, secondary bile acids). Mouse studies link the microbiome to α-synuclein aggregation and to behaviour, an active (and sometimes overhyped) field. Colonic **enterochromaffin cells** make most of the body's **serotonin**, which regulates motility.

**Colorectal cancer biology**: the **adenoma–carcinoma sequence** (Vogelstein): **APC** loss (Wnt pathway activation) → **KRAS** activation → **TP53** loss over years. About 15% of cancers instead arise via **mismatch repair** defects (**microsatellite instability**), as in **Lynch syndrome**; these tumours respond unusually well to **immune checkpoint inhibitors**. **Familial adenomatous polyposis** (germline APC) produces hundreds to thousands of polyps.

**Hirschsprung disease**: failure of **neural crest** cells (RET pathway) to migrate to the distal colon, leaving an **aganglionic** segment that can't relax.
levels.expert:
**Exam**: abdominal inspection and palpation, percussion for distension, **digital rectal exam**. Change in bowel habit, blood in stool, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia and weight loss are **red flags** for colorectal cancer.

**Investigations**: **colonoscopy** is the gold standard (it can also remove polyps); **CT colonography** is an alternative. Screening uses **faecal immunochemical testing (FIT)** and colonoscopy. **Faecal calprotectin** separates inflammation from functional problems.

**Key diseases**:
- **Colorectal cancer**: right-sided tumours often present with **anaemia** and fatigue; left-sided ones with change in bowel habit, bleeding or **obstruction** ("apple core" on contrast imaging). Staged by TNM; treated with surgery (**right hemicolectomy**, left hemicolectomy, sigmoid colectomy), plus chemotherapy in selected patients.
- **Diverticular disease**: outpouchings mostly in the **sigmoid**; **diverticulitis** gives left iliac fossa pain and fever ("left-sided appendicitis"), diagnosed on CT.
- **Ulcerative colitis**: continuous inflammation starting at the rectum, bloody diarrhoea; risk of **toxic megacolon**. **Crohn's** can also affect the colon with skip lesions.
- **Volvulus**: a twisted **sigmoid** gives a "**coffee bean**" sign on X-ray; caecal volvulus also occurs.
- **Ischaemic colitis**: at watershed areas, with "**thumbprinting**" on imaging.
- **Large bowel obstruction**: absolute constipation, distension; a competent ileocaecal valve creates a **closed loop** with risk of caecal perforation (danger when the caecum is over about 10–12 cm).

**Neuro relevance**: **spinal cord injury** above the sacral segments causes **neurogenic bowel**, needing a structured bowel programme; injuries above T6 risk **autonomic dysreflexia** triggered by bowel distension. **Cauda equina syndrome** disrupts S2–S4 control. Constipation is a common early non-motor sign of **Parkinson disease**, sometimes years before tremor. Neuro-ICU patients often get **acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)**.

keyPoints: ~1.5 m: caecum, ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid
Taeniae coli, haustra and fatty tags identify colon
SMA supplies to the distal third of transverse; IMA beyond
Splenic flexure is a watershed area for ischaemia
Absorbs water and salt; houses the gut microbiome
Red flags: blood, changed habit, anaemia, weight loss

test.q: Which part of the colon is a watershed area between the SMA and IMA?
test.explain: The splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) lies between SMA and IMA territories.

test.q: The three bands of longitudinal muscle on the colon are the ______ coli.
test.explain: Taeniae coli are shorter than the colon wall, pulling it into haustra.

test.q: Which short-chain fatty acid is the main fuel for colonocytes?
test.explain: Bacteria ferment fibre into butyrate, which colon lining cells burn for energy.

test.q: An X-ray shows a huge 'coffee bean' loop. Likely diagnosis?
test.explain: A twisted sigmoid colon fills with gas and forms a coffee-bean shape.

test.q: Absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon is ______ disease.
test.explain: Neural crest cells fail to reach the distal bowel, so that segment can't relax.
